description: Bit manipulation exploits binary structure — XOR self-cancellation, AND/OR masking, shifting, and two's-complement identities — to solve problems in O(1) space or to compress exponential state into a single integer. It appears both as a standalone trick and as the enabling substrate for bitmask DP in Hard-rated problems.
important_details: XOR is its own inverse: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, so XOR-ing a whole collection cancels every paired value.
n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit; n & -n isolates it. These two identities underpin most counting and traversal tricks.
A bitmask over n items enumerates all 2^n subsets, making n <= 20 a strong hint that a bitmask solution is intended.
Java has no unsigned int: use >>> for logical right shift and be careful with the sign bit when iterating all 32 positions.
Bitmask DP compresses 'which items have been used' into one integer index, turning permutation search into polynomial-per-state DP.
other_relevant_details: Recognition signals: constraints with n <= 20 or 22, phrases like 'appears once/twice/three times', explicit XOR/AND/OR in the statement, or a requirement of O(1) extra space where counting would naturally need a map. Always sanity check operator precedence in Java — comparison binds tighter than &, so conditions like (x & 1) == 1 need those parentheses.

variations.description: Find the one element appearing an odd number of times when all others appear exactly twice, by XOR-ing the entire collection so pairs annihilate.
important_details: XOR is commutative and associative, so the order of traversal is irrelevant — pairs cancel wherever they sit.
The same idea finds a missing number: XOR all indices with all values, and only the missing one survives.
Achieves O(1) space where a HashMap frequency count needs O(n) — that space reduction is the entire point of the question.
Extends to finding the XOR of a range or detecting a single mismatch between two arrays.

problems.name: Find the Original Array of Prefix Xor

variations.description: When every element except one appears exactly k times, count set bits at each of the 32 positions modulo k; the leftover bits reconstruct the unique element.
important_details: For each bit position 0..31, sum that bit across all numbers and take the result mod k — non-zero remainders belong to the unique number.
Handle negative numbers: after building the result, if bit 31 is set, the value is already correct in two's complement in Java.
The alternative is a two-variable state machine (ones, twos) using ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones — O(1) space and very fast, but hard to derive under pressure.
The counting version generalizes to any k, while the state machine must be redesigned per k — prefer counting unless asked for constant-variable space.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(32n) = O(n). Space: O(1).

problems.name: Number of Valid Words for Each Puzzle

variations.description: When exactly two elements appear once and all others twice, XOR everything to get a^b, isolate any set bit of that result, and use it to split the array into two groups each containing one unique element.
important_details: Any set bit in a^b is a position where a and b differ — that bit is a perfect discriminator for partitioning.
Isolate the lowest set bit with xorAll & -xorAll, which is the cleanest way to pick a discriminating bit.
XOR each group separately; the pairs still cancel within their group, leaving a and b.
Two passes over the array, O(1) space — the HashMap solution is O(n) space and is what this is meant to improve on.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) across two passes. Space: O(1).

problems.name: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

variations.description: Count set bits efficiently using Brian Kernighan's n & (n-1) loop for a single number, or a DP recurrence to build a full 0..n table in linear time.
important_details: Brian Kernighan: each n &= (n-1) removes exactly one set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit rather than 32 times.
DP recurrence dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) reuses the already-computed answer for i/2 — a neat DP-on-bits result.
An alternative recurrence dp[i] = dp[i & (i-1)] + 1 is equally valid and sometimes easier to remember.
Integer.bitCount() exists in Java, but interviewers usually want the manual derivation.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) for the table, O(set bits) per single popcount. Space: O(n) for the table, O(1) otherwise.

problems.name: Sort Integers by The Number of 1 Bits

variations.description: Recognize structural properties of a number from a single bitwise expression: powers of two, alternating bits, complements, and bit reversal.
important_details: n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) == 0 identifies a power of two, since exactly one bit is set.
Powers of four additionally require the set bit to be at an even position: (n & 0x55555555) != 0.
Complement of a number within its own bit length: compute the mask of all ones up to its highest bit, then XOR.
Bit reversal is done by shifting the result left while shifting the input right, appending the extracted bit each iteration — remember to use >>> to avoid sign extension.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(1) for property checks, O(32) for reversal. Space: O(1).

variations.description: Implement addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division using only bitwise operations, simulating a hardware full-adder with XOR for the sum and AND-shift for the carry.
important_details: Sum without carry = a ^ b; carry = (a & b) << 1. Loop until the carry becomes zero.
Subtraction is addition of the two's complement: a - b = a + (~b + 1).
Division without the divide operator uses repeated doubling of the divisor (binary long division) for O(log n) instead of O(quotient) repeated subtraction.
Overflow is the classic trap in divide-two-integers: Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1 must be special-cased to return Integer.MAX_VALUE.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(32) for addition, O(log n * log n) for division. Space: O(1).

variations.description: Represent each of the 2^n subsets of an n-element set as an integer where bit i means 'element i is included', enabling exhaustive enumeration without recursion.
important_details: Iterate mask from 0 to (1<<n)-1; test membership with (mask & (1 << i)) != 0.
Only feasible for n up to roughly 20, since 2^20 is about a million and 2^25 is already too slow.
Encoding a word's character set as a 26-bit mask makes 'do these two words share a letter' an O(1) AND test — the trick behind maximum-product-of-word-lengths.
Enumerating all SUBMASKS of a mask uses the idiom for (int sub = mask; sub > 0; sub = (sub - 1) & mask), which runs in O(3^n) across all masks and is essential for set-partition DP.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^n * n) for full enumeration, O(3^n) for all submask enumeration. Space: O(2^n * n) for stored output.

problems.name: Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique Characters
Number of Valid Words for Each Puzzle
Count Number of Maximum Bitwise-OR Subsets

variations.description: Use a bitmask as a DP dimension representing which items or nodes have been used, turning factorial-time permutation search into O(2^n * n) or O(2^n * n^2) dynamic programming.
important_details: dp[mask][i] usually means 'best cost having covered exactly the set mask, currently positioned at i'.
Transitions add one unset bit at a time: newMask = mask | (1 << j) for each unvisited j.
Iterate masks in increasing order so that every predecessor state is already final when you read it.
Popcount of the mask often encodes 'how many items are placed', which lets you index a second dimension implicitly rather than storing it.
Feasible only to roughly n = 20; beyond that, look for a greedy, flow, or approximation formulation instead.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^n * n^2) typical. Space: O(2^n * n).

variations.description: Generate sequences where consecutive entries differ by exactly one bit, using the reflect-and-prefix construction or the closed form i ^ (i >> 1).
important_details: Closed form: the i-th Gray code is i ^ (i >> 1) — a one-line generator for the whole sequence.
Reflection construction: take the previous sequence, mirror it, and prefix the mirrored half with a 1 bit. This is the constructive proof of correctness.
Gray codes show up in circular-arrangement problems and in hardware/encoder contexts where single-bit transitions matter.
Verify your output by checking that the popcount of (a ^ b) is exactly 1 for every consecutive pair, including the wraparound pair.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^n). Space: O(2^n) for the output.
